title: India Today Investigation Exposes Sprawling Fake Dairy Racket Across Delhi-NCR
excerpt: Undercover reporting reveals synthetic paneer, adulterated milk, and fake khoya flowing into restaurants and street vendors, raising alarm about food safety enforcement gaps.
body:
• An India Today investigation has exposed a network producing and distributing fake paneer, adulterated milk, and synthetic khoya across Delhi-NCR.
  • In a separate Noida bust, police seized 14 quintals (1,400 kg) of fake paneer made with starch, chemical whiteners, and non-food-grade substances that had been sold to eateries for six months.
  • The FSSAI has launched a nationwide crackdown on dairy adulteration, targeting production units, wholesalers, and restaurants with stricter licensing checks.
  • Health experts warn that consuming adulterated dairy products can cause food poisoning, allergic reactions, and long-term organ damage.

An India Today undercover investigation has exposed a sprawling network of fake dairy production across Delhi-NCR, documenting how synthetic paneer, adulterated milk, and counterfeit khoya are manufactured in unlicensed facilities and distributed to restaurants, sweet shops, and street vendors across the national capital region.

The investigation comes amid a broader surge in dairy adulteration cases across India. A recent report by the Authentication Solution Providers' Association and CRISIL found that counterfeiting cases in the dairy sector have increased 2.5 times, with dairy products emerging as the most targeted food category in the country.

How the Racket Works

The production methods documented are disturbing in their sophistication. According to investigators and police reports from a related Noida bust, fake paneer is manufactured by soaking cheap, starch-rich agricultural beans, boiling them, and mixing the paste with chemical whiteners and poster colors to simulate the appearance of genuine cottage cheese. An unidentified blue chemical compound is added to curdle the mixture into paneer-like blocks.

In another method, racketeers use milk powder mixed with water and palmolin oil — an industrial-grade fat — to give the product a creamy finish. The blocks are then shaped with additional chemicals and sold as premium paneer at a fraction of production cost.

Police in Noida recently busted an interstate operation that had supplied fake paneer to eateries across Delhi-NCR for at least six months. Officers intercepted a pickup truck carrying nearly 14 quintals (1,400 kg) of adulterated paneer, which led them to a concealed production unit in Aligarh district. Four suspects were arrested.

Scale of the Problem

The Delhi-NCR racket is not an isolated case. Food safety authorities in Ghaziabad recently intercepted a consignment of over 1,000 kg of suspected paneer packed in plastic drums and being transported in unhygienic conditions. The entire load was destroyed on the spot — buried in a deep pit to prevent it from re-entering the supply chain.

In Hyderabad, a separate crackdown by the Commissioner's Task Force resulted in the seizure of approximately 825 kg of suspected adulterated and misbranded dairy products from 45 outlets and eight manufacturing units in a single operation. Inspectors found cheese analogue being repacked and sold as "Premium Paneer" without proper licensing or labeling.

"On August 3, the regulator issued an order barring Dabur India from selling food products with misleading "100%" claims on products including honey, ghee, and coconut oil, according to Reuters."

Health Risks

Food safety experts warn that consuming adulterated paneer can have severe health consequences. Fake dairy products may contain starch, detergents, urea, non-food-grade chemicals, and non-milk fats that can cause stomach infections, food poisoning, nausea, and in severe cases, damage to the liver and kidneys.

The risk is compounded during summer months, when improperly stored dairy products are particularly vulnerable to rapid bacterial growth.

Regulatory Response

The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has responded with a nationwide enforcement campaign targeting dairy adulteration. The drive covers small dairy units, wholesalers, and retail outlets, with inspectors collecting samples for laboratory testing and verifying licensing compliance.

Hotels, restaurants, catering services, and fast food chains have been warned against procuring or using adulterated dairy products, with penalties including seizure of goods, license cancellation, and criminal prosecution. States have been asked to strengthen inter-state coordination to prevent adulterated products from moving across borders.

The FSSAI has also taken separate action against major brands. On August 3, the regulator issued an order barring Dabur India from selling food products with misleading "100%" claims on products including honey, ghee, and coconut oil, according to Reuters.

What Consumers Can Do

Authorities advise consumers to purchase paneer only from licensed vendors, check labels and expiry dates, and avoid loose or unlabeled dairy products. Simple home tests — such as checking whether paneer crumbles easily or develops a rubbery texture when heated — can help identify suspected fakes, though laboratory analysis remains the only definitive method.
nri_angle: The investigation highlights food safety risks that concern diaspora members who regularly consume dairy products during visits to India and worry about the authenticity of Indian dairy exports.
